result: The SARS-CoV-2 multibasic cleavage site (MBCS) enhances infectivity on Calu-3 lung adenocarcinoma cells but increases infectivity on VeroE6 cells when mutated. Wild-type and mutant pseudoparticles were produced at similar levels, with S1/S2 cleavage observed only in wild-type. MBCS mutations (Del-PRRA, R685A, R685H) increased infectivity 5-10 fold on VeroE6 cells but decreased infectivity 5-10 fold on Calu-3 cells.
evaluation: Claims C30-C37 provide converging evidence from immunoblotting (C30-C32) and infectivity assays (C34-C35) showing differential effects of MBCS mutations on different cell types. The data demonstrate that MBCS mutations functionally destroy the cleavage site (C36) and alter cell tropism (C37), with appropriate controls and quantification shown in referenced figures.

result: The SARS-CoV-2 MBCS facilitates entry into human airway organoids (hAOs). Human airway organoid cultures express ACE2 and TMPRSS2, and SARS-CoV-2 pseudoparticles successfully infected these organoids. Wild-type SARS-CoV-2 was 2-fold more infectious than Del-PRRA and R685A mutants, and 8-fold more infectious than the R685H mutant.
evaluation: Claims C38-C44 demonstrate MBCS function in a physiologically relevant model system. Immunohistochemistry confirms receptor/protease expression (C38-C39), microscopy confirms infection (C41), and quantitative infectivity data (C42-C43) support the conclusion that MBCS facilitates airway cell entry (C44). This represents a key advance over cell line studies.

result: SARS-CoV lacks an MBCS yet infects Calu-3 cells with similar efficiency to SARS-CoV-2, and inserting the PRRA motif into SARS-CoV S did not increase infectivity. This indicates that SARS-CoV S has other adaptations besides the MBCS to facilitate airway cell infection.
evaluation: Claims C45-C47 and C93-C95 provide experimental evidence (infectivity assays) showing that SARS-CoV achieves airway cell infection without an MBCS, and that adding an MBCS does not enhance SARS-CoV infectivity. The inference that SARS-CoV has alternative adaptations (C46, C95) is reasonable given the data, though the specific mechanisms remain unidentified.

result: SARS-CoV-2 exclusively uses serine proteases for entry into Calu-3 cells, while SARS-CoV mainly uses serine proteases but retains some cathepsin-mediated entry. Entry of SARS-CoV-2 pseudoparticles was inhibited by camostat but not E64D, whereas SARS-CoV entry was inhibited ~90% by camostat and ~10% by E64D.
evaluation: Claims C48-C53 present protease inhibitor data demonstrating differential protease usage between SARS-CoV-2 and SARS-CoV. The experimental design using specific inhibitors (camostat for serine proteases, E64D for cathepsins) is appropriate, and the quantitative data support the conclusions about exclusive vs. mixed protease usage.

result: The SARS-CoV-2 MBCS increases the rate of serine protease-mediated entry. SARS-CoV-2 entered Calu-3 cells faster than SARS-CoV via serine proteases. Adding the PRRA motif to SARS-CoV increased entry rate, while removing it from SARS-CoV-2 decreased entry rate.
evaluation: Claims C54, C57-C59 provide kinetic data from time-course experiments showing that the MBCS accelerates serine protease-mediated entry. The gain-of-function (SARS-PRRA) and loss-of-function (SARS-2-Del-PRRA) experiments provide complementary evidence supporting the conclusion that MBCS facilitates faster entry.

result: The SARS-CoV-2 MBCS increases S protein fusogenicity. MBCS-containing S proteins were more cleaved than those without the site. SARS-CoV-2 S was more fusogenic than SARS-CoV S on Calu-3, VeroE6, and VeroE6-TMPRSS2 cells. Inserting the MBCS into SARS-CoV S increased fusion, while mutating the SARS-CoV-2 MBCS decreased fusion. TMPRSS2 expression increased fusion ~2-fold for both viruses.
evaluation: Claims C60-C66 use a GFP complementation fusion assay to demonstrate that the MBCS enhances fusogenicity across multiple cell types. Western blot data (C60) confirms increased cleavage, and quantitative fusion data (C61-C66) from gain- and loss-of-function experiments provide strong support for the conclusion that MBCS increases fusogenicity.

result: SARS-CoV-2 frequently induced syncytia in human airway organoids, whereas SARS-CoV-infected cells rarely contained multiple nuclei.
evaluation: Claims C67-C68 are supported by confocal microscopy and quantification showing differential syncytia formation between SARS-CoV-2 and SARS-CoV in physiologically relevant airway organoids. This provides in situ evidence for enhanced fusogenicity of SARS-CoV-2 in relevant human tissue.

result: The MBCS increases serine protease usage while decreasing cathepsin usage for viral entry. In VeroE6-TMPRSS2 cells with both active pathways, SARS-CoV-2 entry was inhibited ~95% by camostat and not by E64D, while SARS-CoV entry was inhibited ~35% by camostat and ~30% by E64D. MBCS mutations in SARS-CoV-2 increased cathepsin usage, while adding MBCS to SARS-CoV increased serine protease usage.
evaluation: Claims C69-C79 and C100-C101 provide systematic evidence using VeroE6-TMPRSS2 cells that express both entry pathways. The differential inhibitor sensitivity between wild-type and mutant viruses, combined with gain- and loss-of-function experiments, strongly support the conclusion that MBCS directs protease usage toward serine proteases and away from cathepsins.

result: SARS-CoV-2 utilizes serine proteases, but not cathepsins, for entry and replication in human airway organoids. Camostat efficiently blocked infection at 16 hours and reduced replication by ~90% at 48 hours, while cathepsin inhibition (E64D) had no effect. In 2D differentiated cultures, viral titers did not increase after camostat pretreatment.
evaluation: Claims C80-C86, C91, and C126 provide comprehensive evidence from multiple experimental approaches (microscopy, RT-qPCR, viral titration) in physiologically relevant human airway organoids demonstrating that serine protease inhibition blocks SARS-CoV-2 entry and replication, while cathepsin inhibition does not. This establishes the in vivo relevance of serine protease-mediated entry.

result: The SARS-CoV-2 MBCS is an adaptation to serine protease-mediated viral entry that alters tropism, increases fusogenicity, increases entry rate, and increases serine protease usage. This represents the main entry route in vivo and can guide design of entry inhibitors.
evaluation: Claims C87-C90, C92, and C127 represent integrative conclusions drawn from the collective experimental evidence presented in the study. These conclusions are well-supported by the convergence of data from multiple experimental systems (cell lines, organoids) and approaches (infectivity, fusion, kinetics, protease usage, inhibition).

result: SARS-PRRA pseudoparticles (SARS-CoV with inserted MBCS) were partially cleaved, unlike wild-type SARS-CoV. Wild-type SARS-CoV used cathepsins for entry, whereas SARS-PRRA did not.
evaluation: Claims C55-C56 provide immunoblotting and inhibitor data showing that inserting the MBCS into SARS-CoV confers partial cleavage and eliminates cathepsin usage. This gain-of-function experiment supports the role of MBCS in determining protease usage.

result: SARS-CoV-2 appears to have adapted for rapid plasma membrane entry via increased fusogenicity and serine protease-mediated S activation, while SARS-CoV may have adaptations for slower entry.
evaluation: Claim C96 is a reasonable inference from the kinetic and fusogenicity data, but C97 is speculative as no specific mechanisms for SARS-CoV's slower entry are identified or tested. The claims represent interpretations rather than direct experimental findings, and alternative explanations are not excluded.

result: Most SARS-CoV patients entered the infectious phase after symptom onset, whereas individuals can transmit SARS-CoV-2 before becoming symptomatic.
evaluation: Claims C98-C99 are supported by multiple citations to published epidemiological studies. However, these are contextual claims from prior work rather than findings from the current study, serving to frame the biological significance of the entry kinetics differences observed.

result: S1/S2 cleavage increases S binding to ACE2, and neuropilins (NRP) may be additional entry factors for SARS-CoV-2. NRP1 binds furin-cleaved proteins, and MBCS mutants showed reduced NRP1 dependence. The role of NRP1 in promoting S1/S2-cleaved virus interaction with ACE2 versus facilitating entry/syncytium formation remains unclear.
evaluation: Claims C102-C109 accurately report findings from cited studies about ACE2 binding and NRP involvement. However, these are contextual claims from prior work used to discuss potential mechanisms, not findings from the current study. The authors appropriately note conflicting interpretations in the literature.

result: Mutations or deletions in the SARS-CoV-2 MBCS arise in cell culture on VeroE6 cells, indicating selective advantage for MBCS loss in this system. A cell culture-adapted virus with complete MBCS deletion was attenuated in hamsters.
evaluation: Claims C110-C112 are supported by multiple citations documenting MBCS mutations in cell culture and attenuation in vivo. These contextual claims from prior work support the biological relevance of the MBCS for in vivo infection while explaining the increased infectivity of MBCS mutants on VeroE6 cells observed in the current study.

result: Chloroquine blocks SARS-CoV-2 entry into VeroE6 cells but not into cells expressing serine proteases (Calu-3, Vero-TMPRSS2). Since chloroquine acts in the endosome and lung cells express serine proteases, inhibitors blocking endosomal entry are likely ineffective in vivo.
evaluation: Claims C113-C118 accurately report findings from cited studies and draw logical inferences about therapeutic implications. The reasoning that endosomal inhibitors would be ineffective in serine protease-expressing lung cells is sound, though claim C118 represents speculation about in vivo efficacy rather than direct experimental evidence.

result: Camostat inhibits SARS-CoV-2 replication ~90% in human airway organoids and may be effective in vivo. For SARS-CoV, camostat improved survival to 60% in a mouse model while cathepsin inhibition was ineffective, supporting a critical role for serine proteases in vivo. Camostat is clinically approved in Japan for chronic pancreatitis and represents a potential therapy for coronavirus infections.
evaluation: Claim C119 is supported by experimental data from the current study. Claims C120 and C125 represent speculation about therapeutic potential based on the organoid data and prior SARS-CoV studies (C121-C123). While the inference is reasonable, claims about in vivo efficacy (C120) require validation in animal models and clinical trials not performed in this study.

result: SARS-CoV-2 emerged in late 2019 causing the COVID-19 pandemic with over 38 million cases and 1 million deaths by October 2020. It is the third zoonotic betacoronavirus to emerge in two decades after SARS-CoV and MERS-CoV, which did not achieve sustained human-to-human transmission. These viruses originate from bats but can spread to humans via intermediate hosts.
evaluation: Claims C1-C6 provide accurate background information supported by citations and epidemiological data. These are contextual claims establishing the significance of the research rather than findings from the current study.

result: The coronavirus spike (S) protein mediates membrane fusion after receptor binding and proteolytic activation. The S protein consists of S1 (receptor binding) and S2 (fusion) domains separated by the S1/S2 cleavage site. SARS-CoV-2 contains a unique PRRA insertion creating a multibasic RRAR cleavage motif, which is absent in other SARS-related viruses. Cleavage occurs at S1/S2 (by proprotein convertases like furin) and S2' (by serine proteases or cathepsins) sites, with S2' cleavage being crucial for infectivity.
evaluation: Claims C7-C25 provide accurate background information about coronavirus S protein structure, function, and cleavage mechanisms, supported by citations to established literature. These contextual claims establish the scientific framework for the study rather than representing new findings.

result: Prior studies showed that exchanging the SARS-CoV-2 MBCS for the SARS-CoV monobasic site decreased fusogenicity on VeroE6 cells and infectivity on Calu-3 cells. Entry of SARS-CoV-2 pseudoparticles into Calu-3 cells can be blocked by camostat. In most cell lines, SARS-CoV-2 entry appears mediated by endosomal cathepsins.
evaluation: Claims C26-C29 accurately report findings from cited prior studies that motivated the current research. These contextual claims establish the existing knowledge gaps and discrepancies between cell lines that the current study addresses.
